directions: Grow in full sun in a gritty, mineral, extremely fast-draining mix, since this squat caudiciform succulent from the limestone plateaus of central Madagascar rots easily in retained moisture. Unlike the tall columnar Pachypodium lamerei, rosulatum develops a swollen, partly above-ground caudex with short, stubby branches, giving mature specimens a sculptural, bonsai-like presence prized in container culture. Bright yellow, star-shaped flowers appear at branch tips in mid-spring before the leaves emerge, followed by a rosette of narrow leaves through the growing season. The plant is deciduous and fully dormant in winter — withhold water almost entirely once leaves drop and resume only as new growth appears in spring.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

directions: Site in full sun in sandy, gritty, extremely well-drained soil; Kudu Lily is a rocky-outcrop native of South Africa and Mozambique that stays shorter and branches more freely than its Madagascar relatives, forming a thick, swollen, gray-green trunk studded with paired spines. Fragrant white flowers with a pink-flushed throat open at branch tips in late summer and fall, often continuing sporadically while the plant still carries leaves, unlike some of its more strictly deciduous relatives. Reduce watering sharply during the cooler dry season, when the plant may shed some or all of its leaves, and never allow the pot to sit in water. The milky sap is toxic and can irritate skin, so handle cuttings and repotting with gloves.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

directions: Plant in full sun in coarse, mineral, sharply draining soil, keeping the caudex mostly at or just above soil level as it would grow in its native South African Cape veld. Pachypodium succulentum forms a large, mostly subterranean or partly buried tuberous caudex from which thin, sparsely spined, whip-like stems emerge each growing season, dying back to the caudex in winter. Clusters of small pink to red, tubular flowers appear on bare or nearly bare stems in spring before or as new leaves unfurl. It is among the more cold-resilient Pachypodium species thanks to its Cape origin, tolerating brief light chill when kept bone-dry, but should still be protected from hard freezes and wet, cold conditions.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

directions: Grow in full sun in a very gritty, fast-draining succulent mix, watering only once the soil has dried out completely; Arabian Desert Rose comes from the rocky, arid mountains of Oman, Yemen, and Saudi Arabia and develops a comparatively squat, massively swollen, potato-like caudex topped by short, thick branches and rounded, leathery leaves. This dramatic caudex habit makes it a favorite for bonsai-style container specimens, with the trunk often raised and exposed above the soil line to showcase its form. Pink, five-petaled flowers appear at branch tips through the warm months, most heavily in spring and summer. It is highly frost-sensitive and should be brought indoors to a bright, warm location well before nighttime temperatures approach 50°F, and all parts of the plant contain toxic sap that can irritate skin and eyes.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

directions: Provide maximum sun and an extremely mineral, sharply draining soil, since this species is even less tolerant of excess moisture and cold than most other desert roses. Endemic to the Yemeni island of Socotra, where it clings to bare rock, Adenium socotranum develops the largest and most massive columnar caudex in the genus, but grows exceptionally slowly even by Adenium standards, often taking many years to reach flowering size. Clusters of pink, funnel-shaped flowers appear on the upper branches, sometimes on nearly leafless stems, and the plant is treated as a prized, slow-accumulating collector specimen rather than a fast landscape subject. Keep it in a warm, bright, draft-free spot year-round, since it has essentially no cold tolerance and should never be exposed to temperatures near or below 50°F.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

directions: Plant in full sun in gritty, low-fertility, very well-drained soil, and let the soil dry between waterings during the growing season. Native to the grasslands of Eswatini and adjacent South Africa, this desert rose keeps its narrow leaves and flowers repeatedly through the warm summer months rather than producing a single seasonal flush like Adenium obesum or A. multiflorum, and it typically stays more compact with a smaller, less bulbous caudex. Pink to magenta flowers with a deeper throat open continuously on new growth, making it a popular parent species in dwarf hybrid desert-rose breeding. Reduce water and move to a frost-free, bright location well before cold weather arrives, since it has no cold tolerance and all plant parts contain toxic sap.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
